inheritance.notes: Class basics (class, __init__, self, attributes, methods) are B11 and enter via pending concept:classes / concept:constructors on define_subclass; encapsulation (_ and __ conventions) is B11, so multilevel_hierarchies only adds what happens to __private names in subclasses (Helsinki 'access modifiers') and has pending concept:encapsulation. isinstance is introduced here only as the is-a check (define_subclass KP4); if B11 teaches isinstance on its own, the stitching pass should make that a prerequisite. exception_hierarchies takes the B09 handoff (custom exceptions with __init__/attributes, catching a family, handler order) and encompasses raising_exceptions.custom_exceptions. multiple_inheritance (MRO, mixins, diamond super) is non-core, codecademy only. Overriding __str__/__eq__ and other dunders is B11 dunder_methods. Reconciliation: pending concept:classes/constructors resolved to classes.define_methods; isinstance now comes from objects_methods.isinstance_checks (prerequisite of define_subclass); multilevel_hierarchies depends on encapsulation.private_by_convention.

polymorphism.notes: Operator overloading (__add__, __len__, __eq__) is B11 dunder_methods; polymorphism.same_call_different_classes KP4 only shows that built-ins already behave polymorphically. parent_calls_overridden_method is the template-method idea and is the hinge for abstract_classes. Duck typing comes last because it generalises overriding to unrelated classes.

composition.notes: Only Helsinki teaches it ('objects as attributes'), but it is a core design tool, so three core topics. Aliasing of contained objects takes the B06 handoff ('aliasing of objects/attributes is the OOP batch'). has_a_vs_is_a also serves as the 'composition over inheritance' part of object_oriented_design. Linked lists and trees (objects holding objects of the same class) are B15.

abstract_classes.notes: One non-core topic (codecademy introduces it). Uses 'from abc import ABC, abstractmethod' and @abstractmethod as memorised lines, as earlier batches did with imports and decorators. Abstract properties and abstract class methods were left out.

interfaces.notes: Only Boot.dev teaches interfaces, in Go. Python's equivalents are duck-typed interfaces, ABCs and typing.Protocol; both topics are non-core. typing_protocol has empty taught_in (none of the courses teaches Protocol) and depends on tool_mypy (non-core, needs a terminal). The fake-object-for-tests idea is a KP here; mocking libraries were not given a topic. Generics (which 'interfaces comes before') are out of scope.

sum_types.notes: Boot.dev's Functional Programming 'Sum Types' chapter. Variants are plain classes because dataclasses belong to B11 (running in parallel); if B11 teaches dataclasses, the stitching pass may rewrite these examples with @dataclass (and then positional class patterns like Circle(r) work). match class patterns (deferred by B04) live in match_class_patterns, which uses keyword patterns so plain classes work. Union aliases use Shape = Circle | Rect rather than the 3.12 'type' statement. Pending concept:enums for the enum-vs-sum-type KP and concept:classes (which should provide isinstance, per the B02 note).

object_oriented_design.notes: Meta-skill taught as three problem-based core topics (identify classes, refactor procedural code into a class, design collaborating objects). Class basics are B11; the four pillars are owned by their concepts (encapsulation B11, inheritance/polymorphism/abstract classes here). Larger OOP projects (Coffee Machine, Quiz, Turtle Crossing, Helsinki's larger application) are project-shaped and best delivered as multisteps built on these topics. SOLID principles and UML class diagrams were not given topics.

clean_code.notes: Boot.dev's OOP 'Clean Code' chapter. Two non-core problem-based topics; naming and one-job functions are already B05 (decomposition.one_job_per_function), named constants B02 and guard clauses B04 (flatten_nesting), so spot_code_smells links and encompasses those rather than re-teaching them. Linters/formatters are B01 pep8_style.linters_and_formatters. Class naming (CapWords) belongs with B11 classes.

topics.title: Subclasses: classes that inherit from another class
topics.summary: Define class Child(Parent), use the methods and attributes it inherits, add new methods, and check the is-a relationship with isinstance.

knowledge_points.title: A subclass gets the parent's methods
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of calls on subclass objects whose methods all live in the parent.

knowledge_points.title: Adding methods only the subclass has
knowledge_points.practice: Write a subclass with one extra method; predict which calls work and which raise AttributeError.

knowledge_points.title: Move shared code into a parent instead of copying it
knowledge_points.practice: Given two classes with duplicated methods, choose what moves into a parent class and write the class lines.

knowledge_points.title: is-a: a subclass object is also a parent object
knowledge_points.worked_example:
d = Dog("Rex")
print(isinstance(d, Dog), isinstance(d, Animal))   # True True
print(isinstance(Animal("x"), Dog))               # False
Every Dog is an Animal; not every Animal is a Dog.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict isinstance results for objects of parent and child classes.

topics.title: Overriding methods and extending them with super()
topics.summary: Replace an inherited method by defining one with the same name, predict which version runs, and extend the parent's version with super().

knowledge_points.title: A method with the same name replaces the parent's
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for calls on parent and child objects when the child overrides a method.

knowledge_points.title: Lookup order: the object's own class first, then the parent
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Cat(Animal):
    pass

print(Cat().speak())   # ...
Python looks in Cat, finds no speak, and uses Animal's.
knowledge_points.practice: For a parent and two children (one overriding, one not), trace which class's method each call uses.

knowledge_points.title: Extend instead of replace: super().method()
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in super() calls so an override reuses the parent's result; predict the output.

knowledge_points.title: Two override bugs: self instead of super(), and a lost return
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix overrides that recurse forever or forget to return the extended value.

topics.title: Subclass constructors: super().__init__()
topics.summary: Give a subclass its own __init__ that calls super().__init__() to set the parent's attributes before adding its own, and diagnose the missing-attribute bug when it does not.

knowledge_points.title: No __init__ in the child: the parent's is used
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which constructor calls succeed and what attributes the objects have.

knowledge_points.title: A child __init__ replaces the parent's
knowledge_points.practice: Explain the AttributeError in short programs; choose the line that is missing.

knowledge_points.title: Call super().__init__(...) and then add the new attributes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Grad(Student):
    def __init__(self, name, thesis):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.thesis = thesis

g = Grad("Ana", "Graphs")
print(g.name, g.thesis)   # Ana Graphs
Pass the parent the arguments it needs; keep the rest for the child.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a subclass __init__ that takes extra parameters and passes the right ones to super().__init__.

knowledge_points.title: The older spelling: Parent.__init__(self, ...)
knowledge_points.practice: Convert Parent.__init__(self, ...) calls to super().__init__(...); spot a call that forgot self.

topics.title: Class hierarchies: several levels, isinstance and private names
topics.summary: Trace method lookup through a chain of subclasses, check relationships with isinstance and issubclass, and use _protected rather than __private for attributes subclasses need.

knowledge_points.title: Lookup walks up the chain
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class A:
    def who(self): return "A"
class B(A): pass
class C(B): pass

print(C().who())   # A
print(C.__mro__)
# (<class '__main__.C'>, <class '__main__.B'>, <class '__main__.A'>, <class 'object'>)
Python searches C, then B, then A, then object.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace which class supplies each method in a three-level hierarchy where some levels override.

knowledge_points.title: isinstance and issubclass across levels
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(isinstance(C(), A))       # True
print(issubclass(C, A), issubclass(A, C))   # True False
print(issubclass(bool, int))   # True: built-in types form hierarchies too
knowledge_points.practice: Predict isinstance/issubclass results for a drawn hierarchy.

knowledge_points.title: __private attributes are hidden from subclasses; use _protected
knowledge_points.practice: Fix subclasses that fail on double-underscore attributes; choose _ or __ for described attributes.

topics.title: Your own exception families
topics.summary: Build a base exception class with subclasses that carry extra data via super().__init__, catch a whole family by its base, and order except clauses from specific to general.

knowledge_points.title: An exception that carries extra data
knowledge_points.practice: Write an exception class whose __init__ stores a value and builds the message; predict what the handler prints.

knowledge_points.title: A base class for a family of errors
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class BankError(Exception): pass
class InsufficientFunds(BankError): ...
class AccountLocked(BankError): ...

try:
    raise AccountLocked()
except BankError:
    print("bank problem")   # catches every subclass
knowledge_points.practice: Draw (Parsons) a small exception hierarchy; decide which handlers catch which errors.

knowledge_points.title: Specific handlers before general ones
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which handler runs; reorder except clauses so each one can be reached.

topics.title: Multiple inheritance, mixins and the MRO
topics.summary: Inherit from two classes, predict which method wins using the method resolution order, write a small mixin, and follow super() through a diamond.

knowledge_points.title: Two parents: the leftmost wins
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which parent's method runs for different base-class orders.

knowledge_points.title: Reading __mro__
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print([c.__name__ for c in Duck.__mro__])
# ['Duck', 'Swimmer', 'Flyer', 'object']
The MRO is the exact search order Python uses.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the MRO for small hierarchies, then check it against __mro__.

knowledge_points.title: A mixin adds one ability to any class
knowledge_points.practice: Write a mixin method and add it to two unrelated classes; spot a host class missing the attribute the mixin needs.

knowledge_points.title: super() follows the MRO, not just 'the parent'
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed order for diamond hierarchies that chain super() calls.

topics.title: Polymorphism: one call, different behaviour
topics.summary: Loop over objects of different subclasses calling the same method, and replace if/elif chains on a 'kind' value with overridden methods.

knowledge_points.title: The same method call runs each object's own version
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of loops over mixed lists of objects.

knowledge_points.title: Replace if/elif on a type with methods
knowledge_points.practice: Refactor an if/elif function on a kind string into subclasses with an overridden method.

knowledge_points.title: Adding a new kind changes no calling code
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Rect(Shape):
    def __init__(self, w, h): self.w, self.h = w, h
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h

total = 0
for s in [Square(2), Rect(2, 3)]:
    total += s.area()
print(total)   # 10
The loop was not touched; only a class was added.
knowledge_points.practice: Add a new subclass so an existing loop handles it; choose which parts of a program must change.

knowledge_points.title: Built-ins are polymorphic too
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(len("abc"), len([1, 2]), len({"a": 1}))   # 3 2 1
len() and + work on many types because each type supplies its own behaviour.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of len, + and * applied to different built-in types, including the ones that raise TypeError.

topics.title: When a parent method calls self.method()
topics.summary: Predict that self.method() inside a parent method runs the subclass's override, write subclasses that fill in such hooks, and catch the misspelled-override bug.

knowledge_points.title: self.body() runs the object's version, even from the parent
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output when inherited methods call methods some subclasses override.

knowledge_points.title: Trace the calls up and down the hierarchy
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Sales().render()
  render  -> found in Report
  header  -> not in Sales, found in Report
  body    -> found in Sales
Each self.x() lookup starts again from the object's own class.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a trace table of which class supplies each call during a method.

knowledge_points.title: Write the hook, reuse the algorithm
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Inventory(Report):
    def header(self): return "STOCK"
    def body(self): return "3 items"

print(Inventory().render())   # STOCK | 3 items
The parent fixes the steps; subclasses fill in the parts that differ.
knowledge_points.practice: Write subclasses that override only the hook methods needed for a given output.

knowledge_points.title: A misspelled override fails silently
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Sales(Report):
    def bdy(self): return "sales: 42"   # typo

print(Sales().render())   # REPORT | (empty)
No error: bdy is just a new method, and the parent's body still runs.
knowledge_points.practice: Find why a subclass's behaviour never appears and fix it.

topics.title: Duck typing: same method names, no shared parent
topics.summary: Use objects of unrelated classes interchangeably because they have the same methods, recognise the AttributeError when one does not, and keep the method's contract consistent.

knowledge_points.title: No common parent needed
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for loops over objects of unrelated classes; choose which classes a function can accept.

knowledge_points.title: A missing method fails only when called
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Rock:
    pass

Rock().speak()
# AttributeError: 'Rock' object has no attribute 'speak'
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which item in a mixed list raises AttributeError and how far the loop gets first.

knowledge_points.title: Same name, same contract
knowledge_points.practice: Find the class that breaks the shared contract (wrong return or parameters) and fix it.

topics.title: Composition: objects that hold other objects
topics.summary: Store objects (and lists of objects) as attributes, reach through them with chained dots, and write methods that delegate to the parts.

knowledge_points.title: An attribute can be another object
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of chained attribute and method access across two classes.

knowledge_points.title: A list of objects as an attribute
knowledge_points.practice: Write an add method that stores objects in a list attribute; predict expressions like s.items[1].weight.

knowledge_points.title: Delegate: compute from the parts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def total_weight(self):
        total = 0
        for item in self.items:
            total += item.weight
        return total

s.add(Item("shoes", 1))
print(s.total_weight())   # 3
knowledge_points.practice: Write methods that loop over contained objects (total, heaviest, names).

knowledge_points.title: Wrapping a part's method
knowledge_points.practice: Add delegating methods so callers no longer reach through two dots; fix a call that skips a level.

topics.title: Shared parts: aliasing inside objects
topics.summary: Predict what happens when two objects hold the same part, decide whether to create a part inside __init__ or accept it, and copy list arguments to avoid accidental sharing.

knowledge_points.title: Two containers, one object
knowledge_points.worked_example:
book = Item("book", 2)
a, b = Suitcase(), Suitcase()
a.add(book)
b.add(book)
book.weight = 5
print(a.total_weight(), b.total_weight())   # 5 5
Both suitcases refer to the same Item object.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values after changing an object that several containers hold.

knowledge_points.title: Create the part inside, or receive it?
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which design fits a description; predict whether two objects share a part.

knowledge_points.title: Copy a list you are given
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Team:
    def __init__(self, players):
        self.players = players

names = ["ana", "bo"]
t = Team(names)
names.append("cy")
print(t.players)   # ['ana', 'bo', 'cy']
# fix: self.players = list(players)
knowledge_points.practice: Find the aliasing bug in constructors that store a caller's list, and fix it with a copy.

topics.title: Composition or inheritance? has-a versus is-a
topics.summary: Decide between inheritance (is-a) and composition (has-a), recognise inheritance used only to borrow code, and refactor it into composition with delegating methods.

knowledge_points.title: Say the sentence: 'is a' or 'has a'
knowledge_points.worked_example:
A Dog is an Animal       -> class Dog(Animal)
A Car has an Engine      -> self.engine = Engine()
A Library has Books      -> self.books = []
knowledge_points.practice: Classify described relationships as inheritance or composition.

knowledge_points.title: Inheriting to borrow code drags in methods you do not want
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Stack(list):
    def push(self, x):
        self.append(x)

st = Stack()
st.push(1); st.push(2)
st.insert(0, 99)     # allowed, but breaks 'last in, first out'
print(st)   # [99, 1, 2]
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what inherited methods allow; explain why the class is not really an is-a.

knowledge_points.title: Refactor to composition and delegate
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a class that inherits from list or dict to hold one instead, exposing only the needed methods.

topics.title: Abstract base classes: ABC and @abstractmethod
topics.summary: Mark methods that every subclass must provide, first with NotImplementedError and then with ABC and @abstractmethod, and read the TypeError that stops an incomplete class being created.

knowledge_points.title: A placeholder that raises NotImplementedError
knowledge_points.practice: Predict where the error appears; write a placeholder method for a base class.

knowledge_points.title: ABC and @abstractmethod: the base class cannot be created
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the import, base class and decorator for an abstract class; predict which lines raise.

knowledge_points.title: A subclass that forgets a method fails at creation
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Blob(Shape):
    pass

Blob()
# TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Blob without an implementation for abstract method 'area'
The error now comes early, when the object is made.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix subclasses so they can be created; decide which subclasses in a hierarchy are still abstract.

knowledge_points.title: Concrete methods in an abstract class
knowledge_points.practice: Write a subclass that supplies the abstract methods so inherited concrete methods work; predict outputs.

topics.title: Interfaces: depending on methods, not classes
topics.summary: Describe what a function needs from an object as a set of methods, write classes that satisfy that interface, swap implementations (including a fake for tests), and state it explicitly as an abstract class.

knowledge_points.title: An interface is the set of methods the code calls
knowledge_points.practice: List the methods (with arguments and return types) a given function requires from its parameter.

knowledge_points.title: Swap implementations behind one interface
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class EmailSender:
    def __init__(self): self.count = 0
    def send(self, text):
        print("email:", text); self.count += 1
    def sent_count(self): return self.count

print(notify(EmailSender(), "hi"))   # email: hi / 1
An SmsSender with the same two methods works with no change to notify.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a second class that satisfies an interface; choose which classes can be passed to a function.

knowledge_points.title: A fake implementation for testing
knowledge_points.practice: Write a fake class that records calls, and an assert that checks the function under test.

knowledge_points.title: Make the interface explicit with an abstract class
knowledge_points.practice: Turn an informal interface into an abstract base class; find the implementation that is missing a method.

topics.title: Structural interfaces with typing.Protocol
topics.summary: Declare an interface as a typing.Protocol, let mypy check that arguments match it without inheritance, and know what Python checks (or not) at run time.

knowledge_points.title: Declare the interface as a Protocol
knowledge_points.practice: Write a Protocol for the methods a function uses; fill in its type hints.

knowledge_points.title: Matching without inheriting, checked by mypy
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls mypy accepts; fix the class mypy rejects.

knowledge_points.title: At run time a Protocol is only a hint
knowledge_points.worked_example:
greet(Rock())
# runs until s.speak(): AttributeError: 'Rock' object has no attribute 'speak'
Python itself does not enforce the hint; mypy finds the problem before running.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which mistakes are caught by mypy, which by Python at run time, and when.

knowledge_points.title: Protocol or ABC?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ABC: classes must inherit from it; Python refuses to create incomplete subclasses.
Protocol: any class with the right methods fits, including ones you cannot edit; checked by mypy.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose Protocol or ABC for described situations (third-party classes, shared code in the base, enforcement at creation).

topics.title: Sum types: a value that is one of several variants
topics.summary: Model data that is exactly one of a few variants, each with its own fields, as small classes joined by a | type hint, handle each variant, and use an Ok | Err result instead of None.

knowledge_points.title: One class per variant, a union for the whole
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the variants and fields for described data; write the classes and the union alias.

knowledge_points.title: Handle every variant
knowledge_points.practice: Write a function with one branch per variant; predict results for each variant.

knowledge_points.title: Enum or sum type?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Enum: a fixed set of choices with no extra data (Colour.RED, Colour.GREEN).
Sum type: a fixed set of choices where each carries its own data (Circle(radius), Rect(w, h)).
knowledge_points.practice: Classify described data as an enum, a sum type or neither.

knowledge_points.title: Ok | Err: results that explain failure
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a function that returns None on failure to return Ok or Err; predict the result for sample inputs.

topics.title: Handling variants with match and class patterns
topics.summary: Use case ClassName(attr=name) patterns to pick a variant and unpack its fields, reject unknown values with case _, and let mypy's assert_never report a forgotten variant.

knowledge_points.title: case Circle(radius=r) matches the class and binds a field
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def area(s: Shape) -> float:
    match s:
        case Circle(radius=r):
            return 3 * r ** 2
        case Rect(w=w, h=h):
            return w * h

print(area(Circle(1)), area(Rect(3, 4)))   # 3 12
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which case runs and what each name is bound to; convert an isinstance chain to match.

knowledge_points.title: Guards and empty class patterns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
match Rect(2, 2):
    case Rect(w=w, h=h) if w == h:
        print("square", w)
    case Rect():
        print("rectangle")
# square 2
Rect() matches any Rect without binding fields.
knowledge_points.practice: Write guarded cases for special forms of a variant; predict which case wins.

knowledge_points.title: Reject anything else with case _
knowledge_points.worked_example:
case _:
            raise TypeError(f"not a shape: {s}")

area("square")   # TypeError: not a shape: square
Without it, an unknown value falls through and the function returns None.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the bug where an unmatched value silently returns None; add the fallback case.

knowledge_points.title: assert_never: mypy finds the forgotten variant
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from typing import assert_never
Shape = Circle | Rect | Tri   # Tri was just added
    ...
        case _:
            assert_never(s)
# mypy: error: Argument 1 to "assert_never" has incompatible type "Tri"; expected "Never"
knowledge_points.practice: Read mypy errors to find which variant a match is missing, and add its case.

topics.title: Finding the classes in a problem
topics.summary: Read a short problem description and pick out the classes, their attributes and their methods, then write the class skeletons.

knowledge_points.title: Nouns become classes or attributes, verbs become methods
knowledge_points.worked_example:
"A library lends books to members. Each book has a title and can be checked out."
classes: Library, Book, Member
attributes: Book.title, Book.checked_out
methods: Book.check_out(), Library.lend(book, member)
knowledge_points.practice: Sort the words of a problem description into classes, attributes and methods.

knowledge_points.title: Attribute or its own class?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
A plain value (a title, a price) -> an attribute.
Something with several parts and its own behaviour (an address with street, city, postcode and a format() method) -> its own class, held as an attribute.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide for described data whether it should be an attribute or a separate class.

knowledge_points.title: Write the skeleton before the details
knowledge_points.practice: Write class skeletons (attributes and method names with pass) for a short specification.

topics.title: From dictionaries and functions to a class
topics.summary: Recognise procedural code that passes the same dict or globals between functions, and refactor it into a class with attributes and methods without changing behaviour.

knowledge_points.title: The signal: data passed to every function
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which programs would benefit from a class and say what its attributes would be.

knowledge_points.title: Refactor every function that takes the dict at once
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder (Parsons) or write the class version of a dict-and-functions program.

knowledge_points.title: Globals become attributes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
score = 0
def add_point():
    global score
    score += 1
# becomes
class Game:
    def __init__(self): self.score = 0
    def add_point(self): self.score += 1
Two games can now keep separate scores.
knowledge_points.practice: Refactor functions that use global to methods on an object; predict state for two separate objects.

knowledge_points.title: Check the behaviour did not change
knowledge_points.worked_example:
acct = Account("Ana")
acct.deposit(50)
acct.deposit(20)
assert acct.balance == 70
Run the same checks before and after the refactor.
knowledge_points.practice: Write asserts that pass for both the procedural and the class version; find the refactor that broke one.

topics.title: Designing collaborating objects
topics.summary: Split a small program into classes that each own their data, put behaviour in the class that owns the data ('tell, don't ask'), and keep input/output separate from the logic objects.

knowledge_points.title: Put the method where the data lives
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which class a described method belongs in; predict state after a sequence of calls.

knowledge_points.title: Tell, don't ask
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# asking, then changing another object's data:
if card.balance >= price:
    card.balance -= price
# telling the object what to do:
card.pay(price)
The rule about balances stays in one place, inside LunchCard.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite code that reaches into another object's attributes as a method call on that object.

knowledge_points.title: Logic objects do not print or ask
knowledge_points.practice: Move input/print calls out of a class into the calling loop; decide which class a line belongs to.

knowledge_points.title: Wire the objects together
knowledge_points.worked_example:
quiz = QuizBrain([Question("2 + 2 = 4?", "True")])
for q in quiz.questions:
    print(q.text, quiz.check(q, "True"))
print("score:", quiz.score)
# 2 + 2 = 4? True
# score: 1
knowledge_points.practice: Assemble (Parsons) a small program from given classes; predict its output for scripted answers.

topics.title: Spotting code smells
topics.summary: Recognise common signs of hard-to-maintain code (vague names, magic numbers, deep nesting, flag parameters, comments that repeat the code) and apply the matching fix.

knowledge_points.title: Vague names and magic numbers
knowledge_points.practice: Pick out the smells in short functions; choose better names and constants.

knowledge_points.title: Deep nesting -> early exits
knowledge_points.practice: Flatten nested if-pyramids into guard clauses without changing results.

knowledge_points.title: Boolean flag parameters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
report(data, True)    # True what?
# split into two clearly named functions:
print_summary(data)
print_details(data)
knowledge_points.practice: Identify calls whose meaning is unclear and split the function or use keyword arguments.

knowledge_points.title: Comments should say why, not what
knowledge_points.worked_example:
i += 1   # add one to i            (repeats the code)
i += 1   # skip the header row       (explains why)
knowledge_points.practice: Classify comments as useful or noise; rewrite noise comments or replace them with a better name.

topics.title: Refactoring safely
topics.summary: Improve code structure in small steps while tests show that behaviour is unchanged, remove duplication with a parameter, and know when an abstraction is not worth adding.

knowledge_points.title: Refactoring changes structure, not behaviour
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Renaming a variable, extracting a function, replacing magic numbers: refactorings.
Fixing a bug or adding a feature: not refactorings, even if done at the same time.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify described edits as refactorings or behaviour changes.

knowledge_points.title: Tests first, then small steps
knowledge_points.worked_example:
1. Write asserts that pass now.
2. Make one small change.
3. Run the asserts.
4. Repeat; if one fails, undo the last step.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps of a safe refactor (Parsons); find the step in a story where the bug crept in.

knowledge_points.title: Merge near-duplicates with a parameter
knowledge_points.practice: Replace duplicated functions with one parameterised function and update the calls; tests must still pass.

knowledge_points.title: Do not abstract too early
knowledge_points.worked_example: A helper used once, a class with one method and no data, or a parameter nobody varies adds reading cost without benefit. Wait until the duplication is real.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which proposed abstractions are worth making for given code.
